newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan reinforces eastern front against rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sudan reinforces eastern front against rebels.

text.p: Convoys of Sudanese troops rumbled into the Blue Nile town of Damazin on Wednesday to reinforce army units caught short by four days of attacks along the eastern borders of the country.
Sudanese rebels, speaking in Asmara and Cairo, said their forces had advanced to within 80 km (50 miles) of Damazin and were pressing on with an offensive which began on Sunday.
In Cairo the opposition National Democratic Alliance called for a popular uprising and army mutiny to overthrow the Islamist government that took power through a military coup in 1989.
The rebels say they have taken two border towns southeast of Damazin and an army garrison near the eastern town of Kassala.

The Sudanese army says Ethiopia was behind the first wave of attacks and on Wednesday it said the Eritrean government had joined the fray, shelling and attacking the border post at Gotned in conjunction with some of the rebels. The Sudanese opposition in exile says its forces are responsible for the fighting.
Many of the attackers were killed at Gotned for the loss of seven Sudanese soldiers, the army added.

State radio, on a war footing since President Omar Hassan al-Bashir declared mobilisation on Monday, said: "Damazin is receiving convoy after convoy of mujahidin (holy warriors) on their way to the front line." Damazin has the hydroelectric plant that supplies 80 percent of the capital's power.

In Khartoum, a battalion of women on its way to the battle zone paraded through the streets to army headquarters, where Defence Minister Hasan Abdel-Rahman Ali told them the attack in the east was part of a plot against the unity of Sudan.
"The armed forces and all the Sudanese people are capable of responding to the attack and giving the mercenaries a lesson they will never forget," he added.

The government began to report victories by the army, at Chali el-Fil in Blue Nile province and at Hamashkoureb near Kassala. Information Minister al-Tayeb Ibrahim Mohamed Khair said 200 enemy troops were killed at the second battle.

The governor of Blue Nile, Babakir Jaber Kabalo, told a rally in Damazin that "the traitors and enemy" suffered huge losses in men and materiel at Chali el-Fil, which lies south of of the captured border town of Kurmuk.

Sudanese Islamist leader Hassan al-Turabi told Reuters in a telephone interview that the attacks had taken the government by surprise because it had deployed army units on the border with a mission merely to combat smuggling.

He said the army originally had only four battalions along the border but the government was sending at least one more, along with units of the paramilitary People's Defence Forces. A battalion usually has between 500 and 1,000 men.
"Actually it's just a surprise... They (the army) did not expect (to perform) any function other than dealing with contraband across the border," Turabi said from Khartoum.
"The army had four battalions spread over 40 or 50 places... People expected Ethiopia to behave differently," he added.
Turabi, who is the speaker of parliament and the Islamist ideologue behind the military-dominated government, said he was convinced that Ethiopians were doing the fighting.
"The people who escaped from the villages said that they were Tigreans but someone said planes are now taking southerners (Sudanese) to Addis Ababa to replace the Tigreans," he said.
Tigreans, people from the north Ethiopian province of Tigre, made up the bulk of the rebel movement which overthrew Marxist ruler Mengistu Haile Mariam in 1991 and which now runs Ethiopia.

He said that a delegation led by Vice President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh, who arrived in Cairo unexpectedly on Wednesday, wanted to ask the Egyptian government about its decision to let opposition leaders use Cairo as their base.

The two major northern opposition leaders -- former prime minister Sadeq al-Mahdi of the Umma Party and Mohammed Osman al-Mirghani of the Democratic Unionists -- have both been in Cairo for about two weeks.
"They (the delegation) want to speak to the Egyptians...(to ask) is it right to deal with a group attacking Sudan from Ethiopia, which is a violation of international law?" he said.
The National Democratic Alliance, in statements explaining its decision to attack government troops, said Turabi's National Islamic Front (NIF) left them no choice.
The rebels say that they do not intend to advance on Khartoum and that their operations are designed only to pave the way for a popular uprising in the capital.

"The political and military leadership of the alliance... call on all the forces of our people, politicians, students, professionals and members of the armed forces to escalate their struggle, launch the popular uprising and deal the inevitable death blow to the evil NIF regime," one of the statements said.
